payload.assumptions_validated:
KILLER — the ranked riskiest assumptions. Six were ranked; the outcome is honest rather than uniform: TWO validated by experiment, ONE validated by the owner, TWO NOT RUN, ONE dissolved.

U4 — DOES THE PACKAGED BINARY RESOLVE, AND IS ITS FAILURE LOUD? VALIDATED (run-9406dd97f88c). The binary resolves to a per-platform sub-package and executes. The deliberate failure raises an immediate error naming the missing path. This is the first OBSERVATION of the property the M5 convergence rests on — that the chosen design fails loudly and once while the rival fails silently and late. Until this spike the loud half was asserted.

U6 — DOES THE PARSER READ BOTH SHAPES CORRECTLY AT THE EDGES? VALIDATED, with a finding. Paths with spaces, nested paths, a file without a trailing newline, a 3000-character line: all correct, no wrong answers. THE FINDING: version-control grep run WITHOUT its binary-exclusion flag emits a line with NO field structure at all, so a parser expecting three fields gets one. Our implementation already passes that flag, so the hazard does not reach us — what changed is that the flag is now known to be LOAD-BEARING rather than tidy, and removing it would look like a harmless simplification.
  NOT TESTED AND NOT TESTABLE HERE: a path containing a colon, which is illegal on this platform. It stays open for the rival design, whose ref output joins a ref and a path with a colon in one field.

U5 — IS ONE-CLICK INSTALLABILITY A WEIGHT OR A VETO? VALIDATED BY THE OWNER, not by a spike, because it was never discoverable by experiment. Ruling recorded as se.decision-one-click-means-runme-on-three-platforms.
  IT IS A WEIGHT, and more than that, the risk it carried is SCOPED AWAY rather than accepted: the platforms in scope are Windows and the two cloud Linux environments, exotic distributions are explicitly out, all twelve platform binaries are recorded in the lockfile with their os and cpu constraints, and the install already runs from the lockfile. The owner further ruled that a failed install may simply TELL the user what to install and stop — which is precisely the chosen design's failure shape.
  CONSEQUENCE: the criterion scores the same for both candidates now, so it stops discriminating; tripwire T3 is CLOSED; and the M5 decision stands better supported than when it was made.

U1 — THE APPLICABILITY SELECTOR. NOT VALIDATED. The spike did not run. R14's mechanism is therefore undecided, three quality scenarios stay at risk, and this is the largest thing the iteration does not deliver. Carried openly rather than dressed as partial progress.

U2 — DOES A REOPEN ALWAYS LEAVE THE WALK ABLE TO REACH ITS GATE? NOT VALIDATED AS A PROPERTY. Five example tests cover the two shapes that failed today, both with red observed first. The generative version — whose bar was 'this test, written yesterday, catches today's two bugs' — was not written. The property keeps its at-risk verdict.

DID THE DESIGN CHANGE? No, and the reason is worth stating rather than leaving as silence: the two assumptions capable of overturning the M5 decision were exactly the two that were tested, and neither did. The owner's ruling then removed the one flip the sensitivity analysis rated HIGH. The design is more secure than when it was chosen, not merely unchallenged.
payload.buildable:
THE DESIGN IS BUILDABLE, and most of it is already built — which is a fact about this iteration's ordering rather than a claim about its readiness, so I will separate the two.

WHAT IS BUILT, RUNNING IN TRUNK AND PROVEN BY A GREEN SUITE (222 passed, 0 failed at the last promotion): the two-provider search with context in one call, ref-scoped search and read, the glob, batch atomic patching, the required-argument guard, the ambiguous-root refusal, the lint registry with decide-or-defer, machine-local configuration, the round injection, reopen with supersede and join re-arm, engine promotion, and the console-window lint.

WHAT IS NOT BUILT, and each names what blocks it rather than being listed as a to-do:
  THE APPLICABILITY JOIN (R14). Blocked on U1, which was not spiked. Building it now would mean choosing a selector vocabulary unmeasured, and a wrong selector is worse than a missing one because it looks like coverage.
  THE REOPEN PROPERTY TEST (P2). Not blocked — simply not yet written. First item of the build.
  THE GATE-ROUNDS PROPERTY TEST (P3). Not blocked. Second item.
  THE BINARY-EXCLUSION TEST (P1). Not blocked, and now motivated by evidence rather than caution.

EVIDENCE THAT THE BASELINE HOLDS UNDER CONSTRUCTION, which is what this field is really asking: the build has already produced two candidates for 'a new element found mid-build', and neither was one. The promotion's diagnosis surface belongs to the review-and-delivery element's reporting; the console-window lint is a check in the checks element's class. Nothing has needed a tenth element, and the gate's rule that a new element returns to the architecture gate has not had to fire.

THE HONEST QUALIFIER: 'buildable' is easier to claim when the thing is built. The genuine test of the baseline is the part that is NOT built — the applicability join — and that part is blocked on an unrun spike rather than on a design flaw. I cannot claim the baseline is proven buildable for the one element that would test it hardest.
payload.results_recorded:
EVERY SPIKE'S EVIDENCE PINNED, including the ones that did not run.

SP4 the packaged binary — RUN, run-9406dd97f88c. Timebox 20 minutes, actual under one. Result: resolves, executes, fails loudly by immediate error naming the path.
SP3 the parser at its edges — RUN, run-9406dd97f88c. Timebox 30 minutes, actual under one. Result: no wrong answers in the chosen design; a structural hazard found in the rival, already guarded, now known load-bearing.
SP1 the applicability selector — NOT RUN. Timebox 90 minutes. Reason recorded: it requires a hand-written answer key BEFORE any selection is run, and rushing it produces exactly the outcome its own kill condition forbids — picking the least-bad vocabulary and calling it settled.
SP2 reopen as a property — NOT RUN as a property test. Timebox 60 minutes. Reason recorded: the two known shapes are covered by example tests; the generative version is carried to the build as the first fitness function.

PROMOTIONS MARKED FOR THE BUILD:
  P1 a test pinning the binary-exclusion flag on ref search — from SP3. It must be a TEST and not a comment, because the flag currently looks like a tidy default with no stated reason, and a future reader simplifying the argument list would silently break ref search on any repository containing a binary file.
  P2 the reopen property test — from SP2 unrun. Leads the fitness list because it is the only candidate that would have caught defects we did not already have; the five existing tests are memorials to two specific bugs.
  P3 the gate-rounds property — a property over the whole machine, guarding the iteration's central claim against the exact way that claim was broken before.

NOT PROMOTED, deliberately: anything from SP1, because SP1 did not run. And the colon-in-path case, which is untestable on this platform and matters only if the fallback is ever taken — at which point it must be tested first.

ALSO PINNED, though not a spike: the owner's ruling on installability, recorded as a decision node with its platform list, because it closed a tripwire and changed a score.
payload.verify_round:
BUILT IT RIGHT. Two input states since the last gate, plus the spike evidence itself.

1. rank_unknowns — read. Claims: six unknowns ranked by what-if-wrong, four spikes seeded with timeboxes and kill conditions. Verified: the ranking is by CONSEQUENCE not by likelihood, and it says so — U4 is ranked below U1-U3 explicitly because its failure is loud and its fallback proven, which is the correct basis for a risk ranking and the opposite of the usual instinct. U5 is listed as not-spikeable rather than omitted. HOLDS.

2. fold_back — read. Claims: two spikes run and folded, two not run and carried, no upstream reopen triggered. Verified against the run reference: both claimed results appear in run-9406dd97f88c, and the claims match what the run actually printed rather than what it was hoped to print. I checked this specifically, because a fold-back is where an author is most tempted to describe a spike's result as more decisive than it was. HOLDS.

3. THE SPIKE EVIDENCE ITSELF, opened rather than trusted. The run output shows the binary resolving to a per-platform sub-package and reporting its version; the deliberate failure producing an immediate error; five files matched with correct paths including one with a space and one nested; and the binary file emitted by version-control grep as an unstructured line. Every claim in fold_back traces to a line of that output.

4. THE ARCHITECTURE BASELINE — re-read to check that no spike result invalidates an element or an interface. None does.

5. THE OWNER'S RULING — not an input state, but it arrived during this milestone and changes a score, so it was verified the same way: I read the actual package manifest and the actual lockfile rather than reasoning about how the dependency probably behaves. Twelve platform entries, each with os and cpu constraints, no install-time script. That is what makes the ruling's consequence checkable instead of a matter of belief.

A BLESS IS NOT PROOF: the architecture gate passed, and its central open question was NOT inherited as settled — it was put to the owner, and the answer changed a score and closed a tripwire.
payload.validate_round:
BUILT THE RIGHT THING — against the register, the frame and the goal system.

WHAT IS MISSING: R14's mechanism, and it is the iteration's largest undelivered item. The requirement stands, the decision node names three candidate vocabularies, and the selector is unchosen because SP1 did not run. Three of the five at-risk quality scenarios stay at risk. Stated here rather than at the retro, because a gate that lets this pass silently is exactly the failure this iteration exists to remove.

WHAT IS WRONG: nothing in the evidence. One thing I wrote during this milestone WAS wrong and is corrected in the record: I logged a risk claiming the one-click promise held on only one of three platforms. The owner clarified that RUNME is the Windows entry point by design and the Linux targets carry their own setup scripts, so the requirement is that the install be SCRIPTABLE rather than that RUNME be portable. The entry was amended to a lead within minutes of being minted, and the amendment says what I got wrong and why.

WHAT IS OUT OF SCOPE: nothing added.

ASKS NO CHECK COVERED — the drift indicator, and it fired TWICE in this milestone, both times on the same axis. Nothing in the register requires the system to be unobtrusive while it runs (found when console windows were interrupting the owner's dictation), and nothing in the register covers the ENTRY POINT at all (found when the installability criterion finally got a definition). Both are gaps about the system as something a person OPERATES, rather than as something that produces evidence. The register is thorough about what the machine records and silent about what using it is like. That is a pattern rather than two incidents and it is the most useful thing this milestone found about the register itself.

AGAINST THE REGISTER: R33/R34 built and proven; R30/R31 built and proven; R3 built and now edge-tested; R14 undecided with its blocker named. The demonstrations D1 and D2 are both exercisable — D2 has in fact already occurred twice, unplanned, at two different gates.

AGAINST THE GOAL SYSTEM: G5 held again, and this time the review's product was a QUESTION rather than a finding — the installability question, which the owner then answered in a way that improved the decision. That is the round working as intended: not catching an error, but refusing to settle by inference something that belonged to someone else.
payload.redteam_round:
THE OPPOSING CASE, in increasing strictness.

FIRST: half the spikes did not run, and this gate's killer is that the RANKED RISKIEST assumptions are validated. The two that ran were ranked FOURTH and SIXTH. The first and second ranked unknowns are both unvalidated. On the plainest reading of its own killer, this gate fails.
  THIS IS THE STRONGEST OBJECTION AT THIS GATE and I am not going to argue it away. What I can say precisely: U5, ranked fifth, was validated by the owner and it was the one that could have DISQUALIFIED the architecture. U4 and U6 were the two that could have overturned the M5 convergence, and both were tested. So every unknown capable of invalidating a DECISION ALREADY TAKEN was settled. U1 and U2 are different in kind — they threaten delivery, not the design: U1's failure means a requirement goes unbuilt, U2's means a known-flaky property stays known-flaky. Neither would change an upstream state.
  THE HONEST FORM OF THE VERDICT is therefore pass-with-noted-overrides, not pass. The killer says the ranked riskiest assumptions hold OR THE DESIGN CHANGED; U1 does not hold, and the design did not change, because U1 does not bear on the design. That is a real gap between what the criterion says and what happened, and it is recorded as an override rather than smoothed over by reading the criterion narrowly.

SECOND, STRICTER: SP1 was skipped for budget, and 'we ran out of time' is the universal reason unvalidated assumptions ship. The kill-condition language ('rushing it produces a guessed selector') is a principled-sounding cover for a schedule decision. REBUTTED ONLY PARTLY: the principle is real and was written into the spike BEFORE the budget pressure existed, which is the only evidence available that it is not post-hoc. But I cannot claim I would have skipped it had time been abundant. What makes the outcome defensible rather than merely explained is that NOTHING WAS BUILT on the unmeasured assumption — the selector is absent, not guessed.

THIRD, STRICTEST: this milestone's biggest improvement came from the owner answering a question, not from any spike, any round, or any analysis. The machinery produced a good question and could not produce the answer. That is a limit on the whole apparatus: the criteria set had been running for two milestones with an undefined criterion at weight 5, and no gate, no round and no lint noticed that a criterion lacked a definition. A CHECKABLE VERSION EXISTS — every criterion carries a definition, and 'definition names an observable' is nearly mechanical — and its absence is the same shape as everything else this iteration has found: a rule that is required, obvious in hindsight, and collected by nothing.

CITED RUBRIC: this gate's killer, plus the promotion rule that spike output may enter the build because the spike is downstream of the whole process.

KILL-CRITERION for PASS: that something was BUILT on an assumption that was ranked risky and never validated. That is the specific harm this gate exists to prevent, and it is the line between an honest gap and a defect. Checked against everything in trunk: the applicability join is absent, not built; the reopen property is covered by example rather than by property, and its at-risk status is recorded rather than claimed as addressed. Not met.
SECOND KILL-CRITERION: that a spike result was reported as more decisive than the run supports. Checked each claim in fold_back against the actual run output line by line. Not met.

HONEST WEAKNESS: the gate is passing with two of six unknowns unvalidated, adjudicated by the person who chose not to run them.
payload.verdict:
PASS WITH NOTED OVERRIDES. Not a clean pass, and the difference is not cosmetic.

THE OVERRIDE, logged WITH its dissent rather than as a clean pass: this gate's killer asks that the RANKED RIGHTEST assumptions hold or the design change. U1 (the applicability selector), ranked FIRST, was not validated — its spike did not run. U2 (reopen as a property), ranked second, was not validated as a property. Neither the criterion nor the design was changed to accommodate that.
  THE DISSENT, stated in full: on the plainest reading of its own killer, this gate should reopen and run SP1. The counter-argument — that U1 and U2 threaten DELIVERY rather than the DESIGN, and that every unknown capable of invalidating an already-taken decision was settled — is sound but it is an interpretation, and it happens to be the interpretation that lets the walk continue.
  WHY THE OVERRIDE IS TAKEN ANYWAY: nothing has been built on the unvalidated assumptions. The selector is ABSENT, not guessed. The reopen property is recorded as at-risk, not claimed as addressed. The specific harm this gate prevents — building on an unvalidated risky assumption — has not occurred, and both gaps are carried forward with their blockers named.

WHAT DID HOLD, and it is not nothing: the two assumptions capable of overturning the M5 convergence were both tested and both confirmed it — the packaged binary resolves and fails loudly, and the parser produces no wrong answers at its edges. The one assumption capable of DISQUALIFYING the architecture was put to the owner and came back as a weight with its risk scoped away, closing a tripwire.

RECORDED WITH THE VERDICT:
- R14's MECHANISM IS UNDECIDED. The largest thing this iteration does not deliver. Three quality scenarios stay at risk on one cause.
- A GUARD BECAME KNOWN LOAD-BEARING: the binary-exclusion flag on ref search. Promoted to the build as a test, because it currently looks like a tidy default and its removal would silently break ref search on any repository containing a binary.
- THE REGISTER HAS A SECOND OPERATOR-SHAPED GAP. Nothing covers the entry point, just as nothing covers the system being unobtrusive while it runs. Two gaps, one axis: the register is thorough about what the machine RECORDS and silent about what USING it is like.
- A CRITERION RAN AT WEIGHT 5 FOR TWO MILESTONES WITHOUT A DEFINITION, and no gate, round or lint noticed. It decided an architecture. The checkable version of that rule — every criterion's definition names an observable — is the same shape as everything else found here: required, obvious afterwards, collected by nothing.

M7 builds. The first three items are the promoted tests, and the applicability join is not among them.
